utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Unfortunately, Judge Hoepfel is not available today due to other ICTY business that he has to attend to. And it is proposed that today's session be conducted in terms of section -- I beg your pardon, Rule 15 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Is that okay? Thank you very much. Unless anybody has a housekeeping issue to raise, the witness may come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Once again - you may remember this, but it is the duty of the Court to remind you - that you are still bound by the declaration that you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I just have a few more questions to ask you, and I want to ask you some questions about the Vance Plan. You testified on Thursday that "it says literally in the plan that the Republic of Serbian Krajina may hold its own police and military." Now, just to be clear, the Vance Plan in fact makes -- never makes any reference whatsoever to the Republic of Serbian Krajina, correct, it speaks only of the UN protected areas?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republic of Serbian Krajina and parts of Croatian territory outside the RSK constituted the United Nations protected areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But the words "Republic of Serbian Krajina" do not appear in the Vance Plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you that the area --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, please --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- where the RSK was --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Please, just listen to the question. You agree with me that the words, the following words, "Republic of Serbian Krajina," do not appear in the Vance Plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vance Plan did not prejudge the political settlement. Whether it dealt with -- or it did, actually, deal with the introduction of peace in the area, in the war-torn area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, did you not understand my question?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I believe I fully understood your question. The Vance Plan did not prejudge --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me repeat it then and see if I can get an answer to it, please. The words "Republic of Serbian Krajina," that term does not appear in the Vance Plan, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vance Plan implied that there would be the introduction of peace to the war-torn area, that is to say the RSK, and parts of territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you answer my question now, please.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that the Vance Plan spoke literally about things in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, but those words do not actually appear in the plan, right? There's no reference to Republic of Serbian Krajina, because that entity was not recognised. Right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vance Plan did not provide for a political settlement. It did not stipulate whether there was going to be an RSK or an SAO Krajina or whichever other solution. It dealt with the fact that first peace would be introduced to the area, whereupon a permanent political solution would be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to move on, though I'm going to submit that you have not answered the question. But the Vance Plan is in evidence in our case, it's Exhibit 115, so it's -- the Court can make its own determination. Now, with respect about the military, just so we're clear, the Vance Plan says that the military is to be disbanded and demobilised. And it specifically says its personnel shall not wear weapons -- I mean shall not wear uniforms or carry weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think the accused has a note.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Isn't that what it says in the Vance Plan, the military is to be disbanded and demobilised, no uniforms and no weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that's the way it was acted upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact what happened then in response to that provision is that the authorities in the RSK simply shifted all the personnel and weapons from the TO, from the Territorial Defence, over to -- and from the JNA into the police as a way of circumventing the Vance Plan. Isn't that correct? In other words, you turned the police into a military.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, that's not true at all. All heavy weaponry was placed in depots under a double-key system, where one key was held by the TO staffs and the other by the UN forces. The TO did not wear uniforms; it was disbanded. The logistics bases of the TO still existed, but they were manned by people in civilian clothes, as was provided by the Vance Plan. Under all the regulations and international standard procedures, the police was able to carry 12-millimetre calibre rifles and pistols. And in addition to that, they had other equipment for repelling different sorts of demonstrations and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Actually, sir, the Vance Plan specifically said that the police could only carry side-arms, no long weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, side-arms means pistols and automatic rifles, short barrels.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is that what the United Nations thought? Did they interpret the provision that way, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we were not in any way criticised by the United Nations forces in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Well, following on that answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could look at Exhibit 00593994. And this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, this is a report of the Secretary-General pursuant to Security Council Resolution 762 and it's dated the 27th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I believe we only have this in the English, if I'm not mistaken, but there's just one relevant paragraph. If we could go to the second page and zoom in on paragraph 7, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is what the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, can you just tell us the number of the report because it is written very small print on the cover page. It always bears the mark S in the upper right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. It's S/24353, 27 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, and I apologise for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, that's fine. I expected Mr. Perovic, but I'm always happy to see you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So paragraph 7 reads this -- this is what the United Nations is saying on the 27th of July, 1992: "However, the process of demobilisation of the TDF in the sectors has been complicated by the parallel emergence of strengthened police and militia organisations. These groups, designated as 'Special Police,' 'border police,' and so on, are equipped with automatic rifles and, in some cases, with machine-guns, in violation of the provisions of the plan which require that the police be equipped only with side-arms. In many cases these groups have taken over from the JNA or Serb TDF responsibility for manning the front lines. They will have to be withdrawn and disbanded. These matters have been repeatedly taken up with the local authorities, but so far without satisfactory results." Now, having heard that, sir, do you want to change the answer you just gave us that the United Nations never complained about the fact that the police was being turned into a military force and that it was being armed with long weapons, in violation of the plan? Do you want to change your answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, combat vehicles owned by the police had 12.7-millimetre machine-guns mounted on them, and I told you that these are accepted standards. We spoke to Mr. Kirudja about these matters and we agreed that we should reduce the headcount of special police units through a two-phase process. And I stand by my statement that these were police units and not military units. Their internal organisation tasks and uniforms were not those of the military. Their structure was that of a police, and they took up the role of UN forces along the borders. We even agreed that they should be withdrawn further deep into the territory. I don't know whether the Security Council dealt with that particular provision.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, in this report dated the 27th of July, 1992, the Secretary-General is saying that these newly strengthened police and militia organisations had to be withdrawn and disbanded. So the view of the Secretary-General in July 1992 was that the police was -- that the strengthened police was in violation of the Vance Plan. And you agree with that, correct, that that was the view of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I'm quite familiar with this report. It said that the TO was withdrawn and demobilised --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you for a moment, sir? You were familiar with this report at the time; correct? You were aware of this report in July of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was very familiar with the report. We acted upon it --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and again I'm telling you that Mr. Martic and I had this meeting with Mr. Kirudja, where we agreed that these units would be disbanded through a two-phase process. Now, why did this not take place so quickly? That's because we had the Miljevac plateau, we had 600 members --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I interrupted you because you gave this evidence before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit 985.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, on the 18th of September, 1992, there was another report of the Secretary-General. It's in evidence in our case as Exhibit 75, and I'm not going to -- I'm not going to pull it up unless it's necessary. But are you aware that in September of 1992 the Secretary-General submitted another report in which he said that the Vance Plan was continuing to be violated by the creation of new Serb militia forces designated as special police, border police, and so forth. In other words, the violations were continuing, and that he said that in reality these new forces were "paramilitary forces." Were you aware of that report in September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of this report as well. But this report says, among other things, that there were violations on the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, the report is in evidence, so the Court will have an opportunity to read the report. My only question was whether you were aware of it. Do you recall or are you aware of the paragraph, it's paragraph 6, in which the Secretary-General said that the -- these paramilitary units, the police, was engaging in ethnic cleansing. Were you aware of that paragraph in the report in September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the report did not use the term "paramilitary forces," "parapolice," "paramilitaries." I can't remember there being a mention of these parties taking -- of these forces taking part in ethnic cleansing, but I would ask you kindly to show me that portion to refresh my memory because it's been a long time ago. It's been -- it was back in 1992 and we're in 2006 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's fine. The report's in evidence, and it's -- I don't really have any more questions about it. It's in evidence, and if you don't remember it then that's fine. I want to ask you now some questions about the police units. You testified -- you were shown a document, which is now Exhibit 978, which was an order from the Federal Secretary of National Defence, dated the 28th of April, 1992, which established police units in the TO. Do you remember seeing that document in your direct examination and talking about it? April 28th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, and I'm quite familiar with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you must remember, then, that Milan Martic opposed this order and acted to keep the police units within the Ministry of the Interior, right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Martic didn't oppose such an order at all --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay, well --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The federal state provided guarantees to the political leadership of the RSK, with a view to allowing the deployment of the United Nations forces. The guarantees meant that the police units should be established and that the JNA should withdraw to the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Since the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina grew complicated, back in that area only the RSK forces, namely TO and the police force, stayed there. For this reason, the federal state, through the JNA, agreed to establish special police units in order for them -- for those to be common to the Yugoslav state. The political leadership in the RSK found this satisfactory and so did the Minister of the Interior, Mr. Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's look at what really happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could look at Exhibit Number 68, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And as it's coming up, I can tell you that this is a document which is dated the 19th of May, 1992, so it's a few weeks after that order of the 28th of April, 1992, and it's from Milan Martic, and it's about the restructuring of the RSK -- it should be on your screen. It's about the restructuring of the RSK MUP units, overview of the state of affairs and the problems encountered. And he says -- he talks about a meeting in the first paragraph and then he says: "In order to overcome the registered shortcomings, we hereby propose the following." And in paragraph 1 he says: "To cancel the order of the third SSNO administration which set the numerical insignia of the MUP brigade and the HE escadrille, as well as the unequivocal view that these forces are under the command of the RSK national defence, both in peacetimes and in war." And then he makes a new proposal, that the MUP brigade -- this is under 1(a): "The MUP brigades are under the command of the RSK MUP in peacetimes, and in times of war they are to be within the composition of the Serbian army of the RSK and that the special purpose battalion be taken from the Knin MUP brigade, remain under the MUP RSK command in times of war and peace." So he is proposing that that order that you talked about in your direct examination of the 28th of April, 1992, be cancelled and that, in effect, the MUP units -- the special police units come under the authority of the RSK Ministry of the Interior, as he explains here, right? So he did propose the order and he proposed a different arrangement. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It transpires from this document that the then-Minister Martic gave a proposal of his own. He was able to propose other variants as well; however, none of those were accepted. Mr. Prosecutor, the units remained under these numerical codes in existence until they were disbanded on the 30th of November, 1992. Not even the battalion that's mentioned here -- and it bears an incorrect title, it wasn't the special battalion, it was the battalion of the special purpose police units -- because Mr. Martic set up this special brigade which was within the MUP and which stayed in existence until Operation Storm, the month of August. Let me tell you this as well --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, sir, I want to focus, if I may. The reality is that in fact the special police units stayed within the Ministry of the Interior, they were under the command of the Ministry of the Interior, and you, as commander of the special police units, were a deputy minister of the interior of the RSK; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units that were set up as they were, according to the latest instructions I drafted, they carried out tasks from within the police force and were linked to the minister of the interior. And I, as the chief of MUP, would occasionally stand in for the minister of the interior because I was also his deputy. And for a while I in fact stood in for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could just look --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There are a number of documents which pertain to this issue, Exhibit 66, 71 --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But I'm going to ask that we look only at Exhibit 72. And this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is an order from you, from the 1st of October, 1992, from the Republic of Serbian Krajina Ministry of the Interior special police units command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's at the top, if we could just scroll back to the top, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it's about the solemn oath for the police cadets.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could go to the end, please. I mean the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's from you as the deputy minister of the Ministry of the Interior, and that's your name and your signature; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is an authentic document, let me tell you right away, and it is true that in this period of time I held the duty of deputy minister. I think it was for a period of two months. If you need an explanation with regard to these cadets, this was recruitment and training of special police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, the special police units at this time, at the time of this order, were under the authority of the Ministry of the Interior in the RSK; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order has to do with the training of police cadets --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and that is why the deputy minister signed the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The special police units at the time of this order were under the authority of the Ministry of the Interior in the RSK; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not of the special police but of the special purpose units of the police. They were directly under the minister of the interior at the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, that's fine. That's fine. Thank you, sir. I'm going to move on. By the way, in October of 1992 do you know who the minister of the defence was in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister of defence, as far as I can recall, was Mr. Stojan Spanovic, a former JNA member by the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to move on to another topic. You -- you testified about Franjo Tudjman's speech, where he said that the war wouldn't have happened had we not wanted it. Do you remember testifying about that speech? I think it was on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We've had a lot of evidence about that speech in our case, and Defence counsel talked about it in its opening statement in this case. That is a speech that took place on the 24th of May, 1992, in Zagreb in front of a big rally at Ban Jelacic Square, correct, and Tudjman spoke to the crowd on that day, and that's when you say he said those words. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to show you what Franjo Tudjman actually said on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And we actually have the video-clip now of the relevant portion of this speech and if we could play it, please. It's V0006993, and if we could switch to the Sanction, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you see that in fact he does not say, as you claimed, that the war wouldn't have happened had we didn't want it. He does not say that. In fact, what he says, sir, is that they wanted -- they wanted to achieve their goals through peace but that they were ready for war and that they would not give up their goals for an independent Croatia. But he does not say that: "The war would not have happened had we not wanted it." Correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, there are some other Tudjman speeches in which he literally said what I, too, tried to convey as literally --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you told us --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but if you wish --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you told us that the speech was on the 24th of May, 1992, and I just played for you what he says in that speech on the 24th of May, 1992. Are you now going to tell me that it's a different -- you were talking about a different speech after all?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other speeches, but it is clear here as well. He said we had -- we led a war and we won. That was in the last sentence. Perhaps we can put it back on the screen and analyse it a bit. He could have resolved the situation by peaceful means following the constitution of SFRY from 1974, but he didn't want to implement the procedure and the constitutional law because there were some other issues at stake, such as the issue of territory. That's why he headed for a war and an armed rebellion in the then-Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, in your testimony you told us that Croatia was provoking incidents, was provoking conflict, and you said that the corroboration for this claim was the fact that Mr. Tudjman said in his speech in May of 1992 that we would -- there would not have been a war if he had not want it. Now, will you agree with me that that's not in fact what he said, right? Will you agree with me about that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By far, more important is the fact that he led a war, that he carried out an armed rebellion in the territory of the SFRY, ignoring the constitution and the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir, you told us that the corroboration for your claim was this speech that he made. Will you agree with me that you were wrong about that corroboration, that he did not say that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply corroborated the fact that a war was waged by Croatia, or rather, Croatia carried out an armed rebellion in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But Mr. Tudjman did not say what you claimed he said, did he? He said something very different; in fact, quite the opposite of what you said he said. He said that the aim was to achieve the goals through peace. That's what he said, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did say that, I can't deny that. But he also said: We waged a war and we won.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is even more horrific what he said in true fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Oh, really? You're -- you think that what you just saw was more horrific than what you claimed he said? That's your view now?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among the documents in existence I believe you will also find a sentence that I will quote now --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, sir, please, no, I don't want another quote. I want to focus on what you just said. You just said: "What he said was more horrific than -- what he said, in fact, was more horrific than what you had claimed he had said." Is that what you're trying to tell us? Did I understand you correctly, that what we saw in that clip is more horrific than what you claimed he said in that speech?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't understand me well. I will repeat. Compared to the speech in which he says: "We waged a war and won," this was worse than what one could say for the speech itself, because what we had on our hands was an armed rebellion by the Croatian leadership and the then-paramilitary units within the territory of a legitimate state, this being the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Tudjman could have gained independence by peaceful means according to the constitution from 1974; that did not prevent him. As to why he chose to go another way and to choose war and armed rebellion, this was up to their leadership and that was the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir -- okay, I'm not going to get into a discussion about those issues now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this video-clip be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The video-clip is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit Number 986.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to ask you a few questions about the Posavina corridor. You testified in your direct examination about the goals of the Posavina corridor operation and that the corridor had become blocked in the spring of 1992. But in fact, it was long a goal of leaders of the RSK, leaders in the Serbian areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and leaders in Belgrade to establish a land link between the Serb areas within the former Yugoslavia; correct? That was a long-time goal of Serb leaders, dating back to 1991.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prosecutor, sir, there was no obstacle, be it physical or political, between the territories to the west of the Drina and Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia and the RSK on the one hand, and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the other, this being -- comprising Serbia and Montenegro. There was always a link.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But -- and the goal was to control that link and to control and to be able to link together the Serb areas to create one Greater Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in a single document or in a single speech did I ever hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So then you did not --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing needed to be established because there was a free territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you didn't hear the minister of information of the SAO Krajina state in August of 1991 - and we have this in evidence as Exhibit 944 - that "a territorial corridor stretching from Krajina across Bosnia and Herzegovina to Serbia is the obvious solution to uniting the two Serb communities." You didn't hear him say that in August of 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A corridor is a legal term for a passage through enemy territory. It wasn't a corridor. This was a single territory in that area. There were 400.000 people who lived there, and no one had an absolute majority. There were 45 per cent Serbs, 26 per cent Croatians, 26 per cent Muslims, as well as some others. It was part of Bosnia and Herzegovina's territory. In May when Bosnia and Herzegovina was divided, it became part of the Republika Srpska territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Precisely. That's precisely the point. The -- it was -- and it was part of the Bosnia and Herzegovina territory, it was mixed territory, and it was the goal of Serb leaders to control that territory so that the Serb areas would be linked, right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The goals of all of the opposing forces differed. The goal of Croatia --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm interested in --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was to take Posavina under its own control.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My question is about the goal of the Serb leaders. And would you agree with me dating back from 1991 the goal of the Serb leaders was to control the territory that would link together the Serbian -- the RSK -- what was later known as the RSK to Serbia and connecting it with Serb areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was long a goal of the Serb leaders; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with such a goal --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, sir, you've answered the question.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but I wanted to say this on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you not recall that at that Assembly session on the 12th of May, 1992, in Banja Luka, the one that at first you couldn't remember being there but then we later established you were in fact there, and Ratko Mladic gave the speech. Do you remember that Radovan Karadzic gave a speech at that session and he -- it's a famous speech. He outlined the strategic goals of the Bosnian Serb leadership, of the Serbian leadership. And the first goal, I'm sure you recall, was separation of -- separation of Serbs from the other ethnic populations. And the second strategic goal -- and this is in Exhibit 45, it's at page 13 in the English. The second strategic goal was to link together geographically the RSK with the Serbian parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia. Do you remember him saying that, that that was the second strategic goal of the Serb people, May 1992? And the purpose was to achieve an alliance of Serbian states. Do you remember him saying that, sir? You were there.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirmed earlier that I was there, and I still stand by the fact that as far as I can remember that session was held in Prijedor. That was an issue at dispute there --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- we voted on the strategic goals, and one of the goals was the one you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, one goal was to establish a link and to carry out a deblocking process. And no one is disputing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll move on. There -- you testified about orders on crimes from the JNA, that the JNA issued orders not to loot or destroy and that these orders were followed. But that's not true, is it, sir? These orders were regularly violated by the JNA, the TO, and by Martic's police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there were orders in place, that we were controlling. I also did not confirm that there were no negative cases or incidents, but all of them were a process by the military prosecutors and the judiciary. In any society, including that, there is also a portion of the population which is prone to criminal acts. Even today we have prisons and courtrooms full of criminals, even in democratic countries, let alone some other countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The truth is -- sir, the truth is that there was looting and destruction and in some areas murder that occurred. And the truth is that nothing was done to prevent this and nothing was done to punish it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not as you say. I'm telling you that there was arson, looting, individual murders, but also I can say this in full responsibility here that we undertook all possible measures to prevent such incidents. I made an analysis of the military judiciary within the 9th Corps --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We're going to talk about that, sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- out of 337 reports --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We're going to talk about that in just a moment. But following on from what you just said, I want to look at Exhibit 26, please, and this is one of the orders you cited to show that the JNA was instructing soldiers not to commit crimes. And this is -- it's dated the 12th of October, 1991 -- is it on your screen? Okay. Now -- and Defence counsel had you read from the end of the document, but let's look at the beginning of the document. In the second paragraph -- this is from Blago Adzic, the chief of the General Staff of the JNA. In the second paragraph, he talks about: "The army continues to perform its main task of preventing the spread of inter-ethnic conflicts and the recurrence of genocide against the Serbian people of Croatia." In the second paragraph, he talks about: "The behaviour of the Ustasha forces towards units blocked in the barracks and that this is typical genocidal behaviour meant to destroy them and ethnically cleanse Croatia" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Whiting, I'm probably slow on the uptake. I'm not keeping pace with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. It's -- I was reading from -- the first quote was from the second paragraph about the recurrence of genocide, and the next quote was from the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, just so that I'm with you, does the second paragraph starts with the words: "Events have taken a different course," or are you looking at: "In keeping with its constitutional obligations"?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, yes. Yes, I see the confusion. I was talking -- the second paragraph for me was: "In keeping with its constitutional obligations."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's read that. What should we look at?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It says that the army -- at the end there, it says: "The army continues to perform its main task of preventing the spread of inter-ethnic conflicts and the recurrence of genocide against the Serbian people in Croatia." And then the next paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Recurrence of genocide against the Serbian people in -- okay, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then in the next paragraphs it talks about the army performing its duties. And in the first sentence it says: "But the behaviour of the Ustasha forces towards units blockaded in barracks and the Serbian population in Croatia and captured members of JNA and their families represents typical genocidal behaviour meant to destroy them and ethnically cleanse Croatia." And then finally -- just the next paragraph, separated paragraph, that begins: "It is obvious that the war which has been imposed upon the Serbian people in Croatia and JNA by the Ustasha forces and their leadership is not about the conquests of Croatian territory as some peacemakers falsely insinuate and pretend." This is the sentence I'm focussing on: "It is rather from defending parts of the Serbian people from genocide and biological extermination with which they are threatened by resurrected fascism in Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, at the end of this statement by the chief of the General Staff of the JNA he says: Oh, yeah, by the way, don't go and commit any crimes. But isn't the message that is being sent in this first part that the Serb people are imminently threatened with genocide and that the Croat Ustashas are going to wipe them out and commit genocide against them, and isn't that -- first of all, isn't that false; and secondly, isn't that likely to whip up hysteria and fear and anxiety among the Serb people?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prosecutor, sir, you put at least 10 to 15 questions to me here, but I'll do my best to reply as far as I can remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, there are just two --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- First of all --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There were just two questions. The first is --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me see --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- isn't this an exaggeration that is false; and secondly, isn't this likely to whip up hysteria and fear of the enemy among the Serb-pure people and lead to the commission of crimes? Just two questions.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything you read out that was stated by the Chief of Staff is completely correct. There is nothing for me to add or take away. What he was trying to alert people to in this information was the measures that were needed to be taken in the field to protect the Serbian people because there was an imminent threat of genocide by the neo-fascist policy of the new Croatian leadership. And the best proof of that is the conclusion of the Storm offensive in 1995 when the area was ethnically cleansed of the Serbs. Over 400.000 Serbs were driven away. They were stripped of their citizenship, property, savings, their houses were destroyed, and the damage was assessed at 17.5 billion euro in -- at the RSK alone. These are the true facts which testify to the genocidal intent of the Croatian leadership. Nobody could have whipped up the situation. Everything that can be done was to try and warn the people to try and preserve them because their memory of the Second World War was a heavy one when over 650.000 Serbs had been killed by the Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, sir, I do now want to ask you about those criminal complaints. You testified that there were 337 criminal complaints within the JNA. Now, you would agree with me, would you not, that that included all manner of crimes, desertion, fighting, that included all kinds of crimes; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct, Prosecutor. I mentioned the figure from an analysis pertaining to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the period up until the 23rd of October and there were 337 criminal reports. I haven't finished yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir -- well, you've answered my question, that it included all manners of crimes. I want to go back to something about the Posavina corridor. You testified about 12 babies dying, and this, I take it, was in May or -- May or June of 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you a little bit, Mr. Whiting. You say he -- the witness has answered you to -- and accepted that it included all manner of crimes. Where is that mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: He said, "It is correct, Prosecutor." I took that to mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's how I understood his answer. If we could -- and the witness has just nodded his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could go back to the 12 babies. You testified that in relation to those 12 babies that: "All flights had been forbidden by the UN Security Council." That's at 9778. In fact, there was no ban on flights imposed until the 9th of October, 1992, long after the Posavina corridor operation; correct? And that was by UN Security Council Resolution 781.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The flights within the Krajina had been forbidden before that, before the 15th of May -- well, perhaps we can discuss the developments at the Udbina airport and the air force in general. As regards the 12 babies, that was June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir, the UN, the United Nations, did not impose a ban on flights until the 9th of October, 1992, after that event had that occurred. And in addition, there was an exception for humanitarian flights, right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, nobody dared to fly in an area or above an area where there were combat activities, and there were no flights --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and the fact is that 12 babies died because of lack of oxygen supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you told us -- I'm just quoting what you told us in connection with these 12 babies. You said that: "All flights had been forbidden by the UN Security Council." And that is false, right, that's just not true?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received such a request from the local UN forces down in the field, and we dared not fly and we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So now your testimony is that it wasn't forbidden by the UN Security Council; it was requested by local UN forces. That's now your new testimony?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that we did not fly. I know that the Security Council adopted a resolution banning flights, but whether this was the first or the second half of 1992, I don't know. I only know that we -- that the air was off-limits to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you started your testimony by telling us that your memory of dates from this period was very good. You can't remember that the ban on flights occurred on the 9th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The accused has a note. I'm sorry, I didn't know you had seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now you can't remember whether it was the first half of 1992 or the second half of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my memory, this was in the first half of the year. But of course you are free to provide arguments that it was later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, it's -- it's not argument, it's evidence. It's UN Security Council Resolution 781 from the 9th of October, 1992. It's in evidence in our case, I believe. In any event, I'll move on. Now, I just want to be clear about one thing. You did not -- you do not originate from the Krajina region in the RS -- in Croatia. Your origins are in Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So it would not be true to say that only JNA officers who were from the Krajina remained there after the JNA withdrew, because you were not from the Krajina and you remained there; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, my ancestors came from the RSK, from Lika, specifically from the village of Bruvno. They moved to Bosnia in the 19th century. I was born in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. My brothers live in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. I am on the very border. It is only the Una River that divides me from Croatia. My village is on the Una River which is the official border between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. The RSK and Bosnia-Herzegovina were closely connected at the time, and we are today still closely linked to the people living in the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During the years that you remained in the RSK, you were still a member of the VJ, which is how the JNA became known after May of 1992. It's name changed from the JNA to the VJ. And you -- you -- during 1992, 1993, 1994, you remained a member of the VJ; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I was a member of the VJ up until 1994, and I was retired on the 30th of September, 1994, and ever since I was in retirement. But I have to tell you that all of us who temporarily stayed in the RSK, we constituted a 30th personnel centre. And all of our pensionable rights, social welfare rights, health care, schooling of our children, all of these matters we resolved in the FRY through the personnel centre, which constituted a sort of a link between the Main Staff of the Army of the Serbian Krajina and the General Staff of the FRY army or the VJ. This personnel centre had several departments or, rather, several officers there who dealt with these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That's perhaps a little more detail than we needed. But you were paid by the VJ, correct, through the personnel centre?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, as regards the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, the salaries were provided by the government. As far as I know -- but please let me explain and this -- you might find this helpful --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, what would be helpful if you could tell me which government.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you were paid --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I will tell you how.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you were paid by the Republic of Serbian Krajina, not by the personnel centre or by the VJ?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. The government took care of equipping and financing the Army of the RSK. Now, what sort of an agreement was in place between the RSK government and the FRY government is quite a different matter. Most likely the FRY did provide salaries for the active servicemen of the VJ, but it was done on the basis of barter. The RSK is an -- was an affluent country and provided the FRY with agricultural products. There was a large fuel crisis in FRY due to sanctions imposed on them. And the RSK had oil supplies in Djeletovci. It was on this barter system that the economic relations functioned in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Perovic, any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have only several questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Djukic, during cross-examination you also spoke of the illegal arming in the former Yugoslavia in the course of 1990. In connection with this, you also mentioned the SFRY Presidency decision dated 9 January 1991, concerning the disbanding and disarming of paramilitary formations. You said that the Croatian leadership circumvented the decision, worked around it. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And I said and mentioned, described, the way in which this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm not asking you this. I'm interested in something else. Thereafter, in March 1991, what did the then-federal secretary for national defence, Veljko Kadijevic, ask from the SFRY Presidency; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, very well. The then-defence minister General Veljko Kadijevic, who was a Croat by ethnicity, asked that an emergency situation be declared, that the state of an emergency be declared, or rather, a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did the SFRY Presidency in fact take a decision declaring a state of emergency or a state of war?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SFRY Presidency did not declare a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall why this was the case?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no consensus in the Presidency, or rather, they lacked the requisite of members for such a decision. The member from the BH did not vote for such an option, as was also the case with the Macedonian Presidency member, which is why the decision wasn't carried, and of course this was also the position of the Presidency members from Slovenia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What we've just discussed, was this shortly before the resignation of the president of the SFRY Presidency, Borislav Jovic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: The event we just spoke about, did it also happen shortly before the address by Slobodan Milosevic, the video of which we were able to see?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and he presented the powerful and truthful arguments in his speech which were presented in OTP documentation, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your cross-examination you explained that in June of 1991 -- or, rather, the Prosecutor reminded you of this, Stjepan Mesic took up the position of the president of the Presidency of the SFRY as a Croatian representative?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: He held this position until autumn 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Whereupon he returned to Zagreb --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The entire re-direct has been leading. And some of it is in the guise of reminding him about what he testified about before but then it just slides into new questions which continue to be leading, and these last several questions have been leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe my learned friend is contradictory. If I'm reminding the witness of his earlier evidence, then I cannot be leading him in any way. I believe that the objection doesn't stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, if you could just point us to a specific question that is leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, I can, sure. I mean, you see that every answer is: Yes, yes, yes, yes, yes. And at page 30, line 10, you explain that he took up the Presidency, yes; he held this position until autumn 1991, is that correct, yes; whereupon he returned -- it's just every single question is: This happened? Yes. That happened? Yes. Except for the one question: Do you recall why this was the case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right, Mr. Perovic, obviously when you say: "He held this position until autumn 1991. Is this correct?" We don't know if you're reminding him of what he said or not because you are not prefacing it by something that he had said earlier, and on the face of it it is leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was the witness himself who spoke of these matters in response to the answers put to him by my learned friend. These serve merely as reminders of his answers. Now, as for the answers themselves, because they are to the point this doesn't mean that I'm leading him in any way, and I'm in fact trying to elicit to-the-point answers from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just want to get confirmation from you, Mr. Whiting, before I rule, did you ask these things in cross-examination? I may not necessarily remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, some of them I did, yes, for sure. And I just -- maybe -- I mean, there's no reason to re-hash it then, to remind him. Just put the question to him. It hasn't been that long a cross-examination. Maybe the way is -- to solve the problem would be if he just put -- rather than remind him of everything, just if he puts the question to him in a non-leading way that he wants to get.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess that would solve the problem, Mr. Perovic, if you just put questions to him. He knows what he testified about. He knows what he said in chief and he knows what he said in cross-examination. But if we resolve that situation on that basis, this would then be well beyond the time convenient?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, do you know in the summer of 1991 and in the autumn of 1991 who was at the helm of the SFRY Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period of time Mr. Stjepan Mesic was at the helm of the SFRY Presidency, Mr. Stjepan Mesic, whereas he is also known Stipe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall mentioning this in your cross-examination after leaving Belgrade and the duty of the president of the SFRY Presidency, did he address the Croatian parliament; and if so, what did he say?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know very well that Mr. Stipe Mesic, in taking the position of the president of the SFRY Presidency, took an oath that he would respect the constitutional order and the constitution of the country, preserve the integrity and defend the sovereignty of the country in the event of an attack from abroad. He violated the oath he took because he did everything in his power to bring about the break-up of Yugoslavia. Upon returning to Croatia at the session of the parliament which was supposed to declare the end of the moratorium on the declaration of Croatia's independence, he said the following: "I accomplished my mission; Yugoslavia is no more."

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we therefore conclude that the words - and I'm referring to the words spoken in the Croatian parliament - are the words uttered by a man who pledged his loyalty to the SFRY, stating that he would preserve its integrity and sovereignty?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he trampled on that oath and did everything to break Yugoslavia up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move on to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I may, I may be wrong about this but my memory is that the witness testified about these matters not in cross-examination but in direct examination. But I'm sure Mr. Perovic has a cite and could clear it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I respond, I just wish to caution the interpreters that it wasn't Judge Bonomy stating these words but Judge Moloto. As for my learned friend's objection I will say the following. It was precisely during cross-examination that the witness spoke of Mr. Mesic's address to the Croatian parliament, and in that context he quoted his words. I don't have the page reference here, but I'm quite certain of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I just found it. He's right. Yes. I apologise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perovic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: We'll move on to a different topic. In cross-examination there was mention of demonstrations, protests, and later on blockades and attacks on JNA military barracks and installations. I have several questions for you, Mr. Djukic, on this subject. In the course of the summer of 1991, which internationally recognised state existed in the area of the then-Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the summer of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the territory of the former Yugoslavia, the only internationally recognised state was the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this state have its regular armed forces and what were they called?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The regular armed forces included the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of these facts and circumstances, what do the orders of the then-president of Croatia, Mr. Tudjman, one dated 5 May 1991, and the other one 15th September 1991, the latter one relating to blockades and attacks, mean with a view, or rather, in -- with regard to the then-existing legislation?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the meaning of the then-existing legislation, it meant that the Croatian leadership effected an armed rebellion in a legal and internationally recognised Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In answering Prosecution's questions, you spoke of the deblocking of the military installations in Kijevo and then later on in Drnis, Sibenik, and so on. In view of the fact you've just mentioned, which was that at the time the JNA and TO constituted the only regular armed forces, did all these situations involve a conflict between regular armed forces and irregular armed formations?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Constitutionally and legally speaking, this was a conflict between legal, legitimate armed forces of the SFRY and paramilitary and parapolice forces of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In reference to the questions put to you by the Prosecutor concerning the Vance Plan, as it was called, do you recall, or rather, do you know whether the then-RSK leadership was asked its consent of the deployment of the UN forces to the area? Do you know or are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very much aware of this. It was at that point that Mr. Milan Babic was removed from his position because he was opposed to the deployment of the international forces. A new leadership was elected, and that leadership, together with the guarantees provided by the SFRY, or rather, with the FRY agreed to the deployment of the international forces to the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the then-RSK leadership was asked to give its consent to the deployment of the international forces?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A number of meetings were held to that effect, and one of the meetings was held in the territory of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now on the subject of humanitarian flights, you were asked about that by the Prosecutor in the context of the Posavina corridor. Do you know who controlled the air, or rather, where the air control was situated shortly before and during Operation Corridor?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was within the competence of the JNA to carry out air control throughout the territory of Yugoslavia, and I mean the regular units of the JNA. There was the unified system of air control.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know prior to Operation Corridor who provided flight permissions?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the command of the peacekeeping forces which issued flight permissions for humanitarian flights.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Who were you referred to at the time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We applied our requests to sector commands, and they were all forwarded to Mr. Satish Nambiar, to the headquarters in Zagreb, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You were therefore referred to the air control in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Was this the reason why you did not seek permission for -- from the air control?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could not ask for one and we didn't get one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sorry, this strikes me as off the topic which was about whether there was a UN Security Council Resolution on this issue, and it's really new evidence now that's being elicited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think my learned friend is right. My question doesn't have to do about any -- with any resolution. The Prosecutor asked about the possibility to organise humanitarian flights. My question for the witness was what, realistically speaking, these possibilities were and who could they obtain permission for such flights from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- the fact that Defence counsel says: "My question doesn't have to do with the resolution is in my view a concession that it doesn't pertain to what was asked either on direct or on cross. On direct the witness testified that there was a Security Council Resolution prohibiting flights, and I can give the reference to that. It's at 9778. I asked him about the date of that and that it in fact was in October of 1992 and not at the time of the Posavina corridor operation. We had an exchange about that and that was it. So to now elicit new evidence about other restrictions and other problems with flights seems to me beyond what was the issue on direct and on cross-examination, which was really the UN Security Council prohibiting the flight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Counsel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, my recollection is that you had further cross-examined the witness on this area as to why he had shifted from his position in chief and was now saying that it wasn't due to the Security Council Resolution, but it was in fact due to the conditions and the fact that because of what was taking place in the air-space they were not allowed or it wasn't prudent to proceed with the humanitarian aid because of the danger impliedly, and I believe this area might arise that counsel is seeking to go into now in relation to that perspective, or am I not comprehending how the evidence was revealed?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, I think that's right, Your Honour, and I won't press it further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In that event, you may proceed then, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djukic, my last question to you was the fact that you had to apply to the air control in Zagreb on the matter of humanitarian flights was the one that actually made it impossible for you to have any such flights?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And as a result, we were unable to have any humanitarian flights.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And the last thing I'd ask you, you spoke of the aggression by Croatia on the UNPAs, you spoke about Miljevac plateau and other such incidents. My question to you is as follows: Did the UN Security Council on the occasion and in the aftermath of such attacks pass any decisions and did Croatia adhere to them?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After each aggression against the Miljevac plateau, the hinterland at Zagreb and the Flash offensive as well as the Storm, the leadership of the RSK protested and reports were forwarded to the Secretary-General and the Security Council of the UN. For some such acts, Croatia would receive non-binding presidential notice, whereas on other occasions there were forwarded concrete measures which they never implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djukic, I have no more questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this completes my re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. Judge. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: My first question is: When you speak of the FRY, which republics or territories do you speak of?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talk about the state units of the FRY, these being its constituent parts. And the socialist republics were as follows: Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbia, Montenegro, and Macedonia. The only republic of the SFRY which had provinces was Serbia, and the provinces were Kosovo and Metohija in the south and Vojvodina in the north.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I had asked you about the FRY, not the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I may have misunderstood your question. The FRY comprised the Republic of Serbia with the two aforementioned provinces, and the Republic of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, they were essentially Serbian?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both these republics are multi-national. Serbia was a state of its citizens, according to its constitution, because in the Republic of Serbia Serbs form the majority, but there are also national minorities such as Albanians, Hungarians, Russians, Ruthenians, Slovaks, and so on and so forth. As for Montenegro, they had their own composition where Montenegrins formed the majority, but Montenegrins are both Orthodox and Catholic Christians. It also included other minorities such as Muslims, Albanians. What I forgot to mention about the Serbs -- Serbia is that the Muslim population is quite significant there, particularly in a part called Sandzak, which is predominantly Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You have given us the ethnic composition, but in terms of political goals would the goals essentially have been that of the Serbian people? Or let me put it this way: Essentially Serbia was the largest and strongest of those entities; would you agree? Do you agree, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of its size and the number of population, Serbia was the greatest republic in the SFRY and of course within the FRY because it was bigger than Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And isn't it fair to say that in essence was the prior entity, that was the SFRY, broke down, it was the unifying force for those that were left in the FRY. Is that not true?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a federal unit of the SFRY, Serbia was one of the proponents or the link of continuity after the SFRY. The Serb constitution mentions a unified Yugoslavia, within which all goals of various ethnicities were to be met.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the principle of equality based on the old Tito's idea of fraternity and unity. In turn, that means that the Serbs only in that part of the then-Yugoslavia could exercise their statehood rights, but they could do that in Croatia as well and in Bosnia-Herzegovina because they were one of the constituent peoples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: All right. But not only for the Serbs in Serbia, but for the Serbs in the other territories, then Serbia would have been the unifying force. That's correct or am I not correct? No?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you are. First of all, I'm not completely certain I understand you fully, but things were supposed to be done as first seen by the constitution. It is quite normal that members of one ethnicity in various parts of the world have a home unit, a home state. For example, Hungarians who nowadays live in the province of Vojvodina are partially taken care of by Hungary, and this involves the issues of territorial integrity, sovereignty and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Are you saying for a Serb in the RSK, then he would have regarded Serbia as the home, as his root?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that particular Serb in the RSK was part of the constituent people there, then he had a right to decide on his fate. He had the full right to say, I want to leave Croatia and I want to be in Bosnia-Herzegovina as part of the Republika Srpska. That was his right. As to whether that was put into practice or not, well that largely depended on the situation during the civil war in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Or that he wanted to be in Serbia itself, no?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbia never accepted such a position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But then the leadership of the RSK --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. I'm going to speak to you about lifting the siege at Kijevo. The prosecuting counsel had put to you that there was a plan, and you said that, in essence, there was no plan. But what you said is that we agreed with the police and the JNA to secure buses. And what I -- and you went on to say what took place. I understood that to have meant that there was some agreement between the police and the JNA. Now, what was the understanding that those two entities would do in order to effect the siege, the lifting of the siege, and what part was played by each?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there are several questions there. First of all, I said there was no plan in existence. By your leave I want to say this: In the combat rules there are such situations foreseen in which plans are made ad hoc. For example, during the march of a unit or an imminent attack. In UNPA zones we had no indications which would warrant such an activity beforehand. As regards your question, to reduce the tension in the area of Kijevo, the Croatian leadership, through its representatives in the Split police administration, and the command of the military navy sector, on the other hand, reached an agreement that buses will be secured to transport MUP members from Kijevo to Vrlika. We had to go through two buffer zones and cross a check-point at Cviljani where they Serb population organised itself. They put their trucks with their women and children on the road and this was not implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Are you saying that in respect to the lifting of the siege everything just fell into place without any understanding of how each entity, the police and the JNA, would comport itself or how it -- they would act strategically in their joint efforts? It just happened or there was no understanding, if even implicitly or tacitly, as to how the organs should operate? You have told Mr. Whiting that there was no plan; this is why I ask you.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we are talking at cross-purposes. The talks and the negotiation lasted for one month prior to the event in Kijevo on the 26th of August, 1991. The police forces did not follow through the agreement that was made because there was a change of orders overnight. Then what followed was Martic ultimatum. That was not implemented because we wouldn't allow anyone go through our buffer zones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... What were the orders that you had that weren't followed by the police, the ones were not followed that were changed overnight, what were those initially?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What police force do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought the evidence says at line 43, 7, the police forces did not follow through the agreement that was made because there was a change of orders overnight. Then what followed was Martic ultimatum. That was not implemented. So I'm really asking based upon your evidence -- I'm sorry, I'll repeat that. I'm asking based on the evidence that you give.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me clarify. There was an agreement in place that the forces be taken out of the -- out of Kijevo by peaceful means and that one unit of the JNA was to assist in the process. The agreement that was reached, when it was supposed to be implemented, was not implemented by the Kijevo police station. The commander, Ivica Bucic, said that they received another order for them to stay in Kijevo and so they did. Then they made use of that window of opportunity to strengthen the forces and to cause an incident by attacking a unit of the JNA that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: But you've still not really given me what I was asking for, because I was trying to ask you from -- and discover from you from a subjective perspective of the -- the entity that you were a part of from your knowledge what it was that took place and what the understanding was as to what would take place in order to lift the siege. And you don't seem to be able to advise me as to what the understanding was, which is what I wanted to get from you. By peaceful means, yes, but what was it that should have been done or should not have been done, according to what was understood? And what would be the part played by the police as against the JNA or was it combined without any definition or how was it? That is really what I had hoped to understand. Am I not making myself clear to you because you're not responding?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this pertains to the Croatian police in Kijevo, the agreement was that they will be taken out of the village and to Vrlika. If we are talking about the police of the RSK, we had no agreement in place on the lifting of the siege in Kijevo. We didn't allow the RSK police to violate our buffer zones. We wouldn't let them go to Kijevo. That is why Minister Martic could not have executed the ultimatum he set. Eight days passed by. There was an incident caused by the Croatian forces in the area.
