You can see that from my evidence, and if you make an analysis, a temporal analysis of events at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm going to move on. I want to thank you for the moment. And I'm going to go to the Golubic training centre and the special purpose units. Now, you said you knew what was going on and how many persons were trained. And I think you were asked if members of -- persons who were trained at Golubic ended up becoming members of the special police units. And you said: No, as a matter of generality they would not. But you said it was possible that groups of trainees could enter those units. By what process and how would these groups of trainees enter those units, could you please tell me?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll be happy to. In March 1991 the training ground began operating. It was headed by Captain Dragan, or Dragan Vasiljkovic. The training lasted until June and several groups had been trained. They would spend 20 or 21 days there training each. This included men who were neither in the JNA nor in the TO or the police. Those were the people who were at the check-points, which were set up on various roads between towns and villages and between different ethnic groups. Later on from among those people, part of them were sent to the TO, part of them to the Krajina police. And when the special police units of the -- were formed, some of the trainees were joined to those units. Those groups had 80 to 100 men each at training. Simultaneously, in the territory of Croatia there was training organised for such people as well, for their people, and the first group included 1.832 men from western Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were people from western Bosnia-Herzegovina of Croatian ethnicity. I believe you are in possession of such documents. In the questionnaires they had to fill out, they stated they were always against the SFRY and that they were desecrating and destroying the monuments of the -- of the national liberation struggle in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: About what percentage of persons trained at Golubic would have ended up in the special purpose units by the root which you spoke of?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have such information. I cannot be precise. But this was largely on an individual basis. For example, if there were 300 people who had completed training and 20 or 30 per cent -- and you can do your own math in terms of actual numbers, 20 to 30 per cent would go to the units of the police, the regular police that was strengthened in this way. The regular police of the RSK, to my knowledge, in 1994 had less than 4.000 members, 2.000 regular policemen, then some 700 of those who were mobilised, and the rest were civilians. There was also a brigade of theirs which was 500 to 600 men strong and some 200 inspectors or detectives. Therefore, a small percentage of the trainees entered either the regular police, or the TO, or the special police units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge, I have no further questions of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Sir, I'm going to ask you to please listen very carefully to my questions and to please answer to my question and to my question only, okay? Don't create your own questions and answer them because otherwise we will not finish. I'm going to ask you what might, perhaps, be very basic and -- sound very silly question, but I don't remember it being mentioned and you may very well have mentioned this. Of what ethnic origin are you?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My ethnic origin is Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You testified on the first day of your testimony that in August 1991 the municipality of Sinj was excluded from the zone of the 9th Corps and replaced by Gracac and Lika. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality of Sinj was excluded --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes, that's fine, you've answered me. Why was it replaced by Gracac and Lika?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sinj there was a garrison, I've already described that, which was part of the 9th Corps. There was a -- the 316th Motorised Brigade there. Its command was there as well as its depots and a part of the soldiers who acted as couriers to mobilise members of the unit. This composition or this unit was blocked by illegal Croatian forces. Sinj is predominantly Croatian. No mobilisation could have been carried out, but after the deblocking some of the materiel was pulled out, whereas the rest was supplied by the General Staff of the JNA. We were given another zone, or a modified zone, which included an additional municipality, the municipality of Gracac, and this all became the zone of the 9th Corps of the JNA and its command was in Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, you also testified, sir, that the training centre at Golubic that was run by Captain Dragan was used to train the people there in the use of weapons in order to set up barricades and protect Serb population from any attacks by Croatian police. That's what you said sometime on the 20th of October, and you've just said now when you were being asked questions by Judge Nosworthy that people who were there worked on the check-points. Do you remember that? Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So was that the specific objective of the training of these men so that they could man the barricades?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people were pulled out from the place of barricades, trained, and then returned. The barricades were put up spontaneously in 1991, and there were barricades put up by both the Serbs and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just listen to my questions. My question simply was: Was that a specific objective of the training of those men that they go and man the barricades? Now you're saying they were pulled out of the barricades themselves to go and be trained and sent back. So it can be inferred that in fact that was the purpose?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the principle used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. And the training centre at Golubic at the time was under which -- under the control of which ministry?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the training centre fell under the competence of Mr. Milan Babic. I think he was head of the ministry. He took over all the duties, and he approved for Captain Dragan's arrival. Later on he removed Captain Dragan in June after an argument between the two of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What ministry is this? If you say Mr. Babic, I don't know. Mr. Babic is a person, not a ministry. What ministry did these people belong to?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they were part of the Ministry of the Interior, but I don't know who was the then-minister of the interior because they rotated frequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have not asked you who was the minister. I've just said -- asked you: Under which ministry did they fall. And I'm asking you once again, listen very carefully to my question and answer just my question. Don't make any additions. Now --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it not so, sir, that at that time the Ministry of the Interior was under the control of Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you, thank you --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- if he was there throughout the period or if there was Mr. Vjestica as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, you don't know. Now, you also testified - and I think it was on the 20th - talking about the members of your corps who were looting in Drnis. You said: "I wrote notes to the commander of the corps, seeking that measures be taken against perpetrators of that activity." Do you remember that question -- that statement? And by "that activity," you meant the looting of Drnis.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated, and I stand by that now, that there were individual instance of looting, arson, and that I took measures against the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... listening to my question. I'm just asking you if you remember the testimony. Okay. What measures were taken against these people?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the degree of the criminal offence involved, measures were taken whereupon reports, criminal reports, were filed, investigating magistrates were involved, indictments issued, and proceedings instituted. For instance, Lieutenant Pero Baljak was one of the persons involved. I can mention others.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't certain about the family name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Involved in what?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Involved in unlawful activities or criminal offences provided for in the criminal code.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. What became of him --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who were members of the armed forces of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What became of this Lieutenant Pero Baljak?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was sentenced to two and a half years in prison by the military court in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why the military court in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the military court which had jurisdiction over the 9th Corps was located in Split. Split, as well as the court there, was blocked; it couldn't function. For this reason, the 9th Corps relied on the military court of the 2nd Military District in Banja Luka, and in December of 1991 the 9th Corps became part of the 2nd Military District anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What measures were taken against the others who looted?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for some of them, as far as I can remember, they were sentenced to prison. You see, the corps commander had the power to punish soldiers and sentence them to three months in prison or a subordinate commander could sentence them to one month in prison. And we applied those measures wherever we could. This was for stealing vehicles and such activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where can the records of these proceedings be found?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire records of the JNA was packed up and shipped to the General Staff of the JNA before the 19th of May, 1992. Unless it was damaged in the NATO bombing of 1999, that's where you'll still find them in the files of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will I find them there after they've been bombed in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that. I don't know where they are stored and if they exist, but I assume that they are there and can be found there by the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you say they were bombed in 1999, so I would imagine that they went up in flames.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the buildings were not destroyed, but they were damaged. But they were -- but they were damaged in the bombing. They were not repaired because they stand there as witness of the bombing, and I'm speaking of the buildings of the General Staff, of the federal ministry, of the republican Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me take you back to the lifting of the siege of Kijevo. You were asked questions by Judge Nosworthy about the plan. I didn't hear you to really say whether there was or there was no plan. Now, the truth of the matter, sir, is that no such action of that magnitude is taken without a plan. There is a plan, isn't it? There was a plan?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the JNA forces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are not answering --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- are deployed, of course there are different scenarios according to which the army can act. But there was no plan at the time. The plan was designed at the moment the Croatian forces attacked the UNPAs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you understand a plan to mean, the word "plan"?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you had in mind that there was a written order, command, or a mission to the effect that the siege should be lifted and that such a document was produced by a higher-level command and then sent down to the lower-level commands, but there was no such decision. At the point we came under attack, and there are quite a few such situations in the army, we made the decision as to what to do next. And of course this is a process that has to be carefully thought out, and I told you how it was carried out without human casualties, very swiftly. The road was deblocked and a buffer zone introduced. And I told you that I was proud of the fact that neither side suffered casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that what you understand the word "plan" to mean?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our military terminology that I was taught in the military schools, and I completed the highest military schools, this is what the plan is understood to mean. You have to have a mission, you have to have a disposition of forces in time and in space. There was no such plan. There isn't even a written document, a decision, stating: I hereby order, I have decided, go ahead, charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you had a disposition, if I may borrow your words, of forces in time and place by virtue of having your forces in time and place in buses travelling to what -- to where you were going to uplift the siege. Isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. I said that there were forces in time and in place as buffer zones separating two ethnic areas, and there was six such zones --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just listen to my question. You did say when you were asked questions by Judge Nosworthy that some of your forces were transported in buses. Didn't you say that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that, not at all. Please. I said that the 9th Corps of the JNA was given the assignment to assist in the pulling out of the MUP forces from the Kijevo police station which were to be taken out on buses. But I told you that they didn't accept this, and this took place one month before the siege of Kijevo was lifted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, let me -- okay. Maybe you are correct. Let me -- as I read what you said. You said: "As records your question to reduce the tension in the area of Kijevo, the Croatian leadership, through its representatives in the Split police administration and the command of the military navy sector, on the other hand, reached an agreement that buses will be secured to transport MUP members from Kijevo to Vrlika."

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, because in Civljani we had people there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just stop. Listen to my question. I've just read you what you said to Judge Nosworthy, and I wanted you to confirm. And you've confirmed, you said "da." My question to you is: The agreement that buses be secured to transport the MUP members from Kijevo, Vrlika would constitute the plan of executing the lifting of the siege, is it not, sir? That's part of the plan. Part of the plan is that the MUP is going to be transported by bus to Vrlika. Isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't the part of the plan. That was the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- short-term task, a task which should not have taken longer than an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And how many other tasks were there? How many other short-term tasks were there?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was one task, and when this did not materialise the other task was to send 9th Corps representatives to the police station and that they should deal with all the matters between the 9th Corps and the Kijevo police staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... listen to my question. My question is: How many other short-term tasks were there? I expect your answer to give me a number. One, two, three, a million, a billion, something like that. Or I don't know --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am utterly at a loss. I don't understand your question at all, and I don't see what you mean by these tasks. Every day the unit's main task was to prevent inter-ethnic conflicts; that was the main task. And all the other tasks stemmed from the main one. The task was to introduce peace and prevent inter-ethnic conflicts. There were other tasks. At the time we provided escorts to -- to ensure that medical supplies came from Split, Vrlika, to Kijevo. Our task was to provide the people in Kijevo with humanitarian aid. We were being referred to by the local Serbs as traitors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to try again to see if I can't get you to understand what I'm trying to say. You also said in your -- in answer to questions by Judge Nosworthy that the police forces did not follow through the agreement that was made because there was a change of orders overnight. Now, two things I would like you to tell me: What was the agreement and what were the orders that were changed overnight and how -- what -- how were they changed, those orders overnight, and what were those orders?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer to your first question, to your first question, is as follows. The task --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, no --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- which the 9th Corps had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. My question was: What was the agreement, not the task? Listen to my question. What was the -- what was the agreement. The police forces did not follow through the agreement. What was that agreement?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement was that the 9th Corps should provide buses and ensure safe passage for MUP members, not people themselves, but for MUP members, and there were 50 of them in order for them to be evacuated to Vrlika or to Split. And this order, or rather, this agreement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Between whom and whom was this agreement? Who were the parties to this agreement?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement was reached by the command of the navy district and the representatives of the Split MUP, and this was probably done with the consent of the top Croatian leadership on the one hand and the JNA leadership on the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait a minute, just -- you did. Don't worry. And what orders were these that were changed overnight?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our orders didn't change; rather, the Kijevo police station issued an order whereby they were not to comply with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Listen to my question. I'm quoting your evidence. You said: The agreement that was made did not follow through because there was a change of orders overnight. Now, I'm asking you very simply: What orders are these that were changed overnight? Don't say to me: Our orders didn't change. I'm asking you -- I don't know whose orders these are. Tell me the orders that changed irrespective of who they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was quite specific and clear in saying that the Croatian leadership changed the agreement and ordered MUP members not to move out but to remain on the premises of the Kijevo police station until further notice. When we showed up with our buses they told us, Sorry, we have orders telling us that we should not move out. We introduced peace and we tried to maintain contact with them by sending negotiators who were representing us until tensions escalated and the JNA buffer zones came under attack. Therefore, during that night our orders were to put the conditions in place for them to safely pull out and to make sure that no harm came their way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You know, what I find very interesting in your evidence is that you say that you were going to lift the siege by peaceful means and you didn't attack until you were attacked. If you are going to lift the siege by peaceful means, why do you have the JNA there? Why don't you have politicians there to say: Guys, please, move off. Here are buses, go to Vrlika. Why is the JNA -- are the JNA forces there to be attacked in the first place if you are coming peacefully? You maintain peace through use of force?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that we were in the buffer zone and maintaining peace and, to a large extent, we managed to maintain peace. We prevented large-scale incidents. Now, as to your question why were we involved, behind our backs and towards Sinj there were three villages, Gornji and Donji Civljani, and Cetina, where people tended to gather and there were provocations, incidents. We pleaded with them. The corps commander went there to personally remove the barricade that they had erected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You either have an answer to my question or you don't. Are you able to answer my question?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I gave you my answer. We had the task of preventing ethnic conflicts in the area. Pursuant to the agreement, we tried to merely assist the forces in safely pulling out of the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that your answer? Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my answer and that was the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. So you are not able to answer me why you lift a siege peacefully by using armed forces and not sending politicians? Because you answered the question that you put to yourself; you are not answering my question.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had politicians wanted peace, they would not have engaged the Yugoslav People's Army to play a role in the settlement of the Yugoslav crisis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my question. My last question to you is: You said today as you were being asked questions, again by Judge Nosworthy, as part of your answer at page 39 today, lines 1 to 5: "Croatia would receive non-binding presidential notice, whereas on other occasions they were forwarded concrete measures which they never implemented." What did you mean by that? I don't understand what are presidential -- non-binding presidential notice.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In these -- in the presidential notice, Croatia was alerted to some actions which were not in keeping with the resolutions. It was criticised, but this did not prevent them from further engaging in such activities; namely, three or four aggressions on the UN protected areas, after the deployment of the international forces there. If ethnic cleansing of UNPAs was acceptable, as was the aggression of the Croatian forces, then what sort of system was really put in place in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me put clarity into my question in case you didn't understand. This presidential notice came -- where did it come from, the president of what who gave the notice?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Secretary-General who issued such presidential notice, whereas the Security Council passed resolutions. I can give you several examples. When Croatia allowed Muslims to be mobilised --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just a second. Just listen to my questions. I just want to know of what institution this president is who is issuing presidential notice. Now you say it is the Secretary-General. The Secretary-General of what?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking of the Security Council of the United Nations and the UN Secretary-General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, is this the president of the United Nations who is sending this or is it the Secretary-General of the United Nations who is sending these notices, these presidential notices?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After resolutions of the United Nations were passed, then there would be such presidential notices. We'd hear over the radio, for instance, that Croatia was given such a presidential notice not to engage in such conduct anymore. After the aggression on the Zadar hinterland, the Croatian forces were supposed to pull out of the area, which they didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, why were these -- why do you mean they were non-binding, these presidential notices?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the frequency of such aggressions on the United Nations protected areas was evident. You had the Miljevac plateau, Medak pocket, Western Slavonia through Operation Flash, and then the final operation, which was Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I guess it's a convenient time to take a break. We'll come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djukic. Mr. Perovic, any questions arising from the questions from the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Further examination by Mr. Perovic:

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Djukic, His Honour Judge Moloto asked you something about the barricades. My question concerning that is as follows. Based on your knowledge and experience as a professional soldier and from the aspect of the military doctrine, what barricades mean, what can be their sole nature in principle?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Barricades are obstacles on roads, bridges, in a street, which prevent communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: To be precise, barricades, by their nature, can they be offensive or defensive only?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are exclusively defensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A question concerning the events of removing the obstacles for communication and flow of traffic through Kijevo. You were asked about this by His Honour and you explained that between the Croatian side and the JNA there was an agreement that had been reached. Did I understand you correctly - and please correct me if I didn't - that the Croatian side changed its attitude towards the agreement overnight and that they gave up on the pulling out of the MUP personnel from the police station in Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been trying to explain that all along. This is correct. They gave up on the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Compared to that point in time, the lifting of the siege in Kijevo, when did that occur, after how much time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, a month elapsed from the initial agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the giving up of the Croatian side on the agreement was not the reason for your action on Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, just a couple of questions. Further cross-examination by Mr. Whiting:

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Just to follow on with respect to the agreement, the so-called agreement. As I -- I understand the goal of the agreement was to -- that the MUP station in Kijevo would essentially be dismantled and the MUP policemen would -- the 50 or so MUP policemen would leave Kijevo. That was what was being sought in this so-called agreement, right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And, sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the cause of tension and that was supposed to have been resolved by peaceful means.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And that was exactly what Milan Martic demanded occur in his ultimatum of the 18th of August, 1991, that the MUP station be dismantled; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at that time. There had been an agreement previously in June --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- for the station to be emptied.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: But the ultimatum of the 18th of August demands the same thing, that the MUP station be dismantled in Kijevo; correct? Or do you not remember what it says?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very well. After the agreement, several incidents occurred. I mentioned them here. And the then-Minister Martic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the -- are you able to answer yes or no does the ultimatum demand the same thing, yes or no, that the MUP station be dismantled? If you can't answer, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the incidents, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Okay. You were asked about proceedings against members of the JNA in Banja Luka who engaged in looting and destruction. In fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is a reference, I'm referring to Exhibit 972.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In fact, there was a very small number of individuals in the JNA who were prosecuted for crimes committed against Croat persons or property in 1991, very small number. Isn't that, in fact, true, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV DJUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct, because we had undertaken measures for its prevention.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Those are all my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Djukic, this brings us to the end of your testimony. The Chamber would like to thank you for taking the time off to come and testify at the Tribunal. You are now excused. You may stand down. Once again, thank you so much for your time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before the Defence calls the next witness, we would like to hear your guidance or position as regards our motion concerning 92 ter. We filed it urgently today, and in that motion we expressed our position and interpreted the Rules in a way that the Defence be made able to introduce statements with some witnesses who can be examined in chief and the OTP would have the opportunity to re-examine those witnesses. This is all in keeping with the Rules. Could we please receive your guidance on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber a couple of days ago ruled that it's not going to be discussing motions. You -- it's going to deal the motions in terms of written decisions and filings must be in writing. You say yourself that you filed this today. The Prosecution has to respond to it and then you'll get a written decision. Can you call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence tried to avoid any possible misunderstanding. It is a fairly simple question, albeit of legal importance. And we wanted to know whether it is possible for the Defence to ask this witness in chief as well, to examine this witness in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure -- you see, I haven't read your motion, Mr. Milovancevic, and I think I've just tried to explain to you that a written decision would be handed down once we have heard the opposition's response. Now, you're asking me --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to interrupt. If it's helpful, the Prosecution is prepared to respond orally now, and in fact I can just say that we don't oppose that with this witness. I can give a more general position or more details if you want, but if that helps, that's our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black, this -- during the proceedings of this case the Chamber has given certain rulings, and rulings, together with Rules of Procedure, has to be respected. And irrespective of the position of the Prosecution, I think those Rules must be respected. Now, I'm not quite sure whether we're talking about the same witness that is now standing in court and whether is it appropriate that we talk while he's here. Can I get guidance from you, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, exactly. That was the only reason why we initiated this discussion orally. We received your decision you referred to, and we know this should all be done in writing, through written motions of the OTP and the Defence. But we have a new situation in the proceedings which is urgent, in view of the Defence. The Defence should know in advance before we start with this witness what we should or should not do as regards the Rules. That is why I asked this question now. This relates to the witness before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The point, Mr. Milovancevic, is that don't you think that this submission of yours is on short notice? Surely the Prosecution has a right to respond to it in writing, as the Court has indicated earlier, that all these issues -- rather than us talking like we are talking now and wasting time, we should have gotten the written response of the Prosecution and you would get a written decision from the Bench and we would get on with the job. Now, how are we to deal with a filing that comes today? You knew all the time that this witness was coming, then you should have filed your filing, number one; number two, to look at it, I would have to read it. I haven't read it before, and I see that you're asking that the Defence wants -- intends to perform a short additional direct examination on three topics. Now, again during the Prosecution case this Chamber handed down a ruling to say that in order to obviate the cross-examiner from going at large and arguing that he's cross-examining on issues that were raised in direct examination of a 92 bis witness or a witness who has tendered a statement in writing, the Court is not going to allow any leading of a witness who comes on a written statement, that the witness comes in and he goes straight into cross-examination. That is mentioned not only on the standards governing the presentation of evidence understood, but it was also a specific order when you, Mr. Milovancevic, were cross-examining a witness of the -- of the Prosecution and the question arose: Are you cross-examining on what the witness had said or are you just cross-examining at large, and we -- and you said: No, it was because -- you're cross-examining on issues that were raised when the witness was introduced. Now, when -- if this witness takes the stand, I don't see why he should be led. He has written what he has written; he must just be cross-examined based on that order. Now -- and I think we should stick by that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is my impression - and forgive me if I am wrong - that it is not good to discuss these matters before the witness. Perhaps he should be led out as regards the continuation of this argument. Since this does not concern him personally, he could be given a wrong impression. This is a matter of principle, and that is why I would like to have the witness taken out, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I asked you for this guidance a little earlier and you didn't respond to it; this is why I can't understand. May the witness please be excused for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honour, before us we have a 92 ter witness. Last Friday the issue of possibility came before the witness, the issue of the possibility of interpreting that rule in a way which would not make it able for the Defence to examine in chief as regards certain topics. We needn't go through everything mentioned in his statement. Since this was last Friday, we couldn't have filed our motion then; instead, we filed it urgently this morning. It is our position, put briefly, that within the -- within Rule 92 ter there is no clear provision precluding examination-in-chief; that is one thing. Another thing is that the Statute of the Tribunal in its Article 21 guarantees a fair trial for the accused, inter alia, providing opportunity to the Defence to examine witnesses on an equal footing with the Prosecution. The Prosecution had their own 89 witnesses, Rule 89 witnesses, and they were also examined on certain topics. We pointed to such instances in our written filing. We believe that a different interpretation of 92 ter would be contrary to the Rules of Procedure themselves because the Rules foresee examination-in-chief, cross-examination, and re-direct. When it comes to Rule 92 ter, of course this only concerns the topics that have been given prior notice of, and we have given notice of the three topics that we intended to deal with. That is why we initiated this question in such a way. I am sorry to have to do it orally, but the interests of justice cannot only be viewed in -- or discussed in written form due to the lack of time, and I would kindly ask for your understanding on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Milovancevic, you're raising a lot of issues. I think the Chamber is going to rule the following: That the Prosecution is going to respond to this motion and the Chamber will hand down its decision, because you're raising a lot of issues here which I don't think I would like to go into orally right now. Okay. That's the ruling, and it is a ruling that is consistent with the rulings that were made earlier, that motions must come in in writing. The motions will be answered in writing to obviate this waste of time. The guidelines are there and the rules are there. So it will be dealt with in terms of the Rules. You can call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I have a proposal to make --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... because I've ruled now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, you handed down your ruling. I had a proposal to make concerning your ruling that the testimony of this witness commence on Wednesday so that our learned friends from the OTP would in the meantime have a possibility to forward their filing so that the Chamber could rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, call the witness then. If you want to skip this one, call the next witness, the one after.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we haven't foreseen such situation. We don't have a next witness ready; he hasn't travelled to The Hague yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Call the witness that's available. Let's carry on, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that the learned friend from the registry is waiting; therefore, I believe your instruction was to bring in the witness. How should I understand this, Your Honour? Can we examine in chief this witness as regards the three topics or not? Because the OTP did not challenge our proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, you may not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in that case, we would like to withdraw this witness and we will not examine him according to Rule 92 ter and no other witness will be examined according to the provisions of that rule without a possibility to examine them in chief. This is contrary to the rights of the accused, and we have no right to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Milovancevic, I don't understand you. You had elected to proceed by 92 ter, and that comes with a specific procedure that is laid down in the relevant rule; and then you have, more recently and urgently, changed your position in respect of this witness. How would it affect your other witnesses that are to come that are 92 ter witnesses? What could possibly make you say what you have just said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we only asked that our OTP friends be given a possibility to express their views on this delicate issue, whether the Defence can examine in chief any witness brought here under Rule 92 ter. We believe that according to the Rules this is not excluded; quite the contrary, it is in keeping with the Rules and the Statute. Given the situation of us being denied that possibility, without having heard a decision on our filing and we haven't heard the OTP response, particularly having in mind that they consented to such an approach of ours, it would be to the detriment of the interest of our client with this witness and we simply cannot do that, Your Honour. If the Defence is not given the possibility to put questions to this witness according to certain topics, as was the practice with the OTP, then we will hear this witness viva voce and in full. Because it is the Defence's interpretation of this rule that this would be contrary to the interests of our client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: But you not only said that, you went on to say that in respect to your other 92 ter witnesses you would also adopt a course where you would withdraw their status, their current status, and you would adopt a status that would permit you -- for them to give viva voce evidence. Is that what you're saying? I thought that was what you had placed on the record. I'm asking in all good grace what would be the reason in respect of those witnesses. I'm not saying I think it is the correct course that you have adopted, but I could understand what could provoke you to say what you did in respect of this witness. But in respect of the others that are to come, now the position is entirely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to stress the position of this Defence. We would like to hear the Chamber's ruling on this issue, and in case that we have to proceed without a prior written decision by the Chamber, and if in case we have to go on with this witness, we do not wish to pursue such a course because if there is a written ruling we can appeal it, and we believe this is a key issue concerning the principles of both the Statute and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence as regards the right to examine in chief. It would seem that we had a complete misinterpretation of Rule 92 ter, and this would apply to the other witnesses that we had foreseen to testify under that rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We thought it was our right to examine on very specific topics that had been notified or communicated to the other party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Let me say something else to you. Now, you, and you alone, the Defence counsel alone, either you yourself as a leader or in consultation with the rest of the Defence team, you would determine how the Defence is conducted subject to any order coming from the Trial Chamber, mm-hmm? At this present time, the Trial Chamber having ruled, as it has done, what is there to stop you from putting the witness up as a 92 ter witness, proper and simpliciter, and permitting him to be cross-examined in the absence of the three areas that is subject to the application pending the decision of this Trial Chamber, in which event you would then know whether or not you could proceed in respect of those areas or not. Us proceeding today with this witness will not avoid or deny you of the opportunity in the future for the Bench to consider your motion properly and to determine whether or not you may, in exercise of the Trial Chamber's discretion, have the opportunity to examine on those areas. And then no time would have been lost. We can proceed and then, I believe, on Wednesday, or sometime during the course of next week you would have that which you are anticipating, or you would have the decision. But I don't think that we should waste today. So my own view is that you could proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with your position, Judge Nosworthy; I believe it to be a fair one. Thank you. From our point of view, this enables us to continue our work. I didn't think of that possibility. I didn't know whether things can go that way, and I would like to accept your proposal and we may continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You know, sometimes we take a decision a little bit rashly from that side of the bar. So, Mr. Milovancevic, I crave everyone's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. The OTP will have no difficulty with that, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: None, Your Honour, that's -- we accept that solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, the witness's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, what I intended to do at this stage was not to put questions. I hope that my learned friend will agree with this. I wanted the Trial Chamber to have the personal background information of this witness because this is something that you cannot see from the summary, and we simply wanted to present this to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You wanted the background for the position of the -- the actual rule itself to be satisfied? You wanted to lay the foundation in relation to the Rule itself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But there's no need for that. I'm sure the foundation is in the 92 ter statement. Doesn't it give his particulars in the 92 ter statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we didn't include the witness's personal background information in the statement. We believed we would be able to do this viva voce with the witness. I simply wanted to go through the personal particulars of this witness and then hand over to my learned friend opposite. And I hope you are agreeable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sure the cross-examiner can elicit that information quite easily. What's your name, what's your address, where do you come from, when were you born, where were you born.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the first 92 ter witness by the Defence. As I understand it, what does have to happen is he has to be presented with the 92 ter statement and adopt that as what he would say if he were to testify orally, to comply with the Rule, and then I can begin cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where is the 92 ter statement? Let's give the witness the 92 ter statement. I would imagine, then, Mr. Milovancevic you would deal with paragraph A3 of Rule 92 ter and that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Her Honour Madam Nosworthy asked me whether I was laying the foundation, and that's precisely what I was doing. I'm presenting you the witness. And I'd like the usher to hand down the statement to the parties to the proceeding and the Bench. I will ask the witness whether this is his statement, and with your permission I can just ask him his particulars and that will be the end of my address at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Milovancevic, I don't know whether the witness -- apparently he sort of had some notes of his own. If you can just also warn him about those notes, that he's not supposed to use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Rules of Procedure are such that do not allow you to use your personal notes during your testimony here. I have just given you the text of your statement that has been -- the copies of which have been given to the OTP and the Bench. Before stating whether this is indeed your statement, tell us, please, your full name.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: Mile Dakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us the place and date of birth and your ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb by ethnicity. I was born in Croatia, municipality of Vojnic, currently municipality of Karlovac. I lived in that area until Operation Storm --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, when were you born?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 9th of May, 1931.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us your educational background and your occupation.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the associate degree pedagogical academy for teacher and then the faculty of philosophy in Sarajevo, and I had been the manager of a memorial site called Petrova Gora. I'm a historian and writer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you held any political positions and do you hold one today?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was the founder of the Yugoslav Autonomous Democratic Party in Croatia in 1990. I was vice-president of the Serbian National Council in Krajina in 1990 and 1991. And as of 1992, I was the president of the state commission for crimes and genocide in -- as it was called at the time with the government of Krajina. Now I am the president of the Association of Refugees from Croatia. I have been holding this position for eight years, and the association is based in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You have the text of a statement before you that was also delivered to the learned friends from the OTP and the Honourable Trial Chamber. Can you tell us, did you give this statement, who you gave it to, and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I gave this statement and I signed each and every page. I gave the statement to lawyer Nikolic, who spoke to me on several occasions, made notes, and that's how the material before me came into existence. I then signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we therefore say that this is your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: This is indeed my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as we are proceeding under the rule for the first time, would it be the right time for me to tender the statement into evidence as a Defence exhibit at this time? Of course this will be up to the Bench to decide upon that. In that case, I wish to tender the statement into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we -- do we have a date on which the statement was given? That would be part of the foundation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was giving the statement on several occasions. As far as I remember, it was early this year. And later on in the course of the year I spoke with lawyer Nikolic. That is how we arrived at the text we have here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, or Your Honour Nosworthy, if I may put the following question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since the statement itself does not bear the date of signature, can you tell us in relation to your arrival here when it was that you signed the statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: I remember signing something for Nikolic as well, but I signed the statement upon my arrival here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And when was your arrival here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I arrived on Saturday in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Was it on the date of your arrival that you signed the statement or on another date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was on the following day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Would that date be Sunday, the 22nd of October, 2006?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I just -- this may seem like a technicality, but I think there's one final tiny hoop to jump through before this can come in. Under Rule 92 ter (A)(iii), before the 92 ter statement can come in the witness has to attest that the statement accurately reflects his reflection, which is what I think he has done, and what the witness would say if examined. I think we should have the record clear on that before the statement is admitted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like to clear that, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I thank my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard what the Prosecutor said, Witness? Can you confirm that the statement is correct and that you would state that which is contained in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: I skimmed through the statement. I can see that there is my signature on each and every page. I wasn't able to read through carefully at this point, but seeing that it bears my signature it is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: There's a question I wish to ask upon looking at the statement. Does the statement bear a declaration? And what is the effect of that fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, can I answer that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rule 92 ter was interpreted by the Defence on the basis of its wording. We, therefore, presume that it isn't necessary that there be a declaration in order for the statement to be tendered into evidence, because the purpose of this rule is the case law before this Tribunal concerning 89(F) and 92 bis. In our view, what 92 ter explicitly asks for is sufficient, and that is for the witness to appear before the Tribunal, state that this is his statement, and this is what his evidence would amount to. And in our view, this is in lieu of the 92 bis declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think the way that Mr. Milovancevic has just stated it is correct. The fact that he's here to orally adopt it is sufficient. I would note that -- maybe it's not worth insisting on. But again, he said: Yes, this is my statement, but I don't believe the record shows that he has said that this is -- this -- what is contained in the statement is what when he would say if he were to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Even before that, I'm just concerned about the fact that the witness says he just cursorily looked at the statement and he assumes it is his statement because of the signature. Now, Witness, I would like you -- you are expected here to say unequivocally - am I right, unequivocally - that this is your statement, this is the statement you would say if you were examined orally in court. You understand that? It's not sufficient to say: I looked at it briefly, I skimmed through it, and I see my signature, therefore it must be my statement. You've got to be able to confirm definitively because you are going to be bound to this statement, you cannot deviate from it any longer, once you have said this is your statement. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is my statement, by all means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if you didn't write it on paper and you were asked orally, you would say exactly what you have said in the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you stand by the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this suffice?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It does, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And I believe the -- it needs to become an exhibit and get a number, Your Honour, just before I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I did think -- yeah, this is the time for it to get an exhibit number. The statement is admitted into evidence, and may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit Number 987.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dakic. Good afternoon, at this point. We're just into the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thanks for your patience as we'll dealt with a couple of procedural issues. You have just adopted the written statement which you see before you as the evidence which you would have given had you testified orally, and so consequently I'm going to ask you several questions about that statement, beginning with a few questions about how it was created, which you've just discussed a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And actually, in the meantime could I ask the usher to lower the ELMO or move the ELMO a little bit because it's just hard for the witness and I to make eye contact. Thank you. I'm grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Dakic, you just told us that you actually signed this statement yesterday here in The Hague. Do I understand correctly that you, yourself, didn't draft this but this was drafted by someone else and then you signed it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to read through the entire statement carefully before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you did that, did you? You went through it --

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: I read it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When did you first provide this information to the Defence? Do you remember when you were first interviewed or first contacted by Mr. Nikolic or someone else from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: It was only Mr. Nikolic who spoke with me and made notes as I spoke. Some of it was drafted back in 2005. I think it was in the autumn of 2005. Later on we met in my office of the Association of Refugees from Croatia. I also recall having been at his home once. He'd always put questions to me and I'd answer them, and definitely I stand by my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks for that explanation. One thing I notice is that the statement has a lot of specific dates and specific numbers in it. Are those dates and numbers that you remember sort of off the top of your head, or did you consult documents or other sources as you and Mr. Nikolic were drafting this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: Well, see, I was an active participant in all these events, and my position was such that I was personally involved in some of these events. Throughout the war, I kept a war diary with all the dates. The diary hasn't been published yet, but I do hope to publish it soon. In addition to that, I authored two books, one of which was published in Knin in 1994, "The Serbian Krajina," and the other which was published in 2002 in Belgrade, "Krajina Through Centuries." The books also contain the chronology of events unfolding themselves in those parts. Therefore, I have to say that I used the information contained in my books and I also recall many of the dates, even though much time has passed since.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And your statement doesn't appear to identify when something is something that you personally experienced and when it's something that you -- that you've based on information from some other source, from your books or from your research for your books. Am I correct about that?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. As I said, I combined the information that was written down with some of my memories, and that's how my statement was produced. I was an eye-witness of many events, especially those taking place in 1990. I spoke with President Tudjman and others because as the president of my party I had frequent contacts with Zagreb. We'd spend time together, and these memories are still fresh in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You mentioned 1990. Where were you in 1991, if you recall? Were you living in Vojnic and did you spend a significant amount of time in any other place during 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: In 1991 I lived in Belgrade for three months. I was exposed to the intimidation from the JNA because the JNA said that they could not save Krajina. And it was on the proposal of a colonel that I went to Belgrade and spent three months there. That is why I was mostly there in 1991 -- oh, I'm sorry actually. That was a slip. I had to flee to Belgrade in 1992, whereas I spent the entire 1991 there. I was the president of the Serbian National Council and an active participant in all the events in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, thank you for that. Let me try to focus and I'd ask you to pay as close attention as possible to my questions because I'm really after just specific information. In this -- for this question, where were you in 1991? You say: "I was" -- "I spent the entire 1991 there." Can you just give us some more details as to where you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: I constantly resided in Vojnic, where I was domiciled. Up until autumn 1991 I was the manager of the memorial site Petrova Gora, and I would go to Knin only to attend the meetings of the Serbian National Council, or else I would go to Srb, Korenica. Oftentimes I would go to Knin for meetings and consultations. But my place of permanent residence was in Vojnic in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any other places besides Knin which you went frequently or spent a significant amount of time during 1991, other than Vojnic where you've explained you resided?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: I'd go to Belgrade in 1991. In that year I was invited by Milosevic to come and meet him in Belgrade. Babic was too. I was the president of this Serb National Council and he was the vice-president, and I recall this meeting taking place in January 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think perhaps we may have had a translation error or there's a misstatement or you can clarify. But what were your position and the position of Mr. Babic on the Serbian National Council in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: Well, the Serb National Council intent -- was working intensely in 1990 --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir --

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: -- in 1991 its activities subsided.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. I was just focussed on what was your position on the council and what was Milan Babic's position on the Serb National Council.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: Milan Babic was the president of the Serb National Council and I was the vice-president. There were two vice-presidents of the Serbian National Council. There was David Rastovic and myself. I wanted to say the following. Already in 1991 the raison d'etre and the significance of the Serbian National Council subsided, especially when in Korenica Milan Babic suggested that Krajina should be annexed to Serbia, and when the referendum was called I was opposed to the idea and we simply parted ways. We were no longer along the same political lines. That was the 12th of May referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You've addressed that in your statement so we don't need to repeat it here. Let me now direct your attention to the statement which I think you have in front of you, and I'm going to ask you about specific paragraphs of the statement, okay? Starting, in fact, with the first paragraph, although it's something that comes up in other paragraphs. You refer repeatedly in your statement to Ustashas and the independent state of Croatia, and you compare the independent state of Croatia to the Croatia of the 1990s in your statement. And my question, sir, is: That was a technique which was used by Serb leaders at the time to create fear in the Serb population, wasn't it, comparing the 1990s Croatian authorities with the fascist authorities of World War II?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you weren't there and you don't know what the situation was like. It was quite rightly that a comparison was drawn with the -- between the independent state of Croatia and the Republic of Croatia. I will tell you what the parallel consists of. Let me just make an aside. It was at a meeting that I said to President Tudjman --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. I don't want to repeat the things that are in your statement; I just want to ask you specific questions. And in this one you've answered, and you said you disagreed with me, so I'm going to move on and ask you specific questions. I don't want to get into too many asides because we have a limited amount of time. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understood your question, and if you wish I will explain to you why it was that we drew a parallel between the independent state of Croatia and the Republic of Croatia. If you want me to, I can explain this. I can explain you where these ties lie, and I can even tell you why there aren't any significant differences between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, actually go ahead and tell me --

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: Can I?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: -- why there are no significant differences between these two governments which existed 50 years separated from one another, if you can do so briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: There are no differences. I hoped when the elections were called back in 1990 in Croatia that as President Tudjman promised me personally we would go back to the authentic origins of Croatia. I told him that in his speeches he should not speak positively about the independent state of Croatia. He told me that after the elections his address would be different; however, after the elections he only became more extreme. I have to say that both the NDH and Croatia outlawed Serbs in many different aspects. Both states banned the use of Cyrillic script. Both states persecuted Serbs and expelled Serbs from Slavonia. This was done both by the NDH in 1941 and by the Republic of Croatia in 1991. Both states adopted a very rigid Croato-centric centralism. The Republic of Croatia adopted the state symbols used by the NDH. We, Serbs, as an equal peoples in Croatia opposed --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, I apologise for the interruption. And we need to keep focussed. And just so you understand the way the procedure works here is that I'll try to ask you questions and if you can respond sort of as focussed as you can on those questions, things will go much quicker. And I'll try to put more focussed questions maybe than that first one. And let me ask you specifically, then, about symbols. In paragraphs 1 and 5, and 17 and I think others of your statement, you talk about symbols. And you -- for one in particular you connect the chequer-board symbol exclusively with the Ustasha movement and the NDH government of World War II. But let me ask you, sir, it's true, isn't it, that that chequer-board symbol was a historical symbol of Croatia and it had been used before World War II in the coat of arms of Kingdom of Yugoslavia; it was used after World War II in the coat of arms of the Socialist Republic of Croatia within the SFRY. It was used by other governments and other regimes besides just the Ustasha regime. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: What you said is partially correct. The truth is that the chequer-board existed before. It existed also with some Serb rulers as back as the 14th century. But the thing is -- well, do you know the fields of the board it starts white/red, white/red. With the Socialist Republic of Croatia, the order was different. I can't recall exactly whether the first field was white or red. In any case, the fields in the Ustasha coat of arms were copied with the new Croatia, and we found that unacceptable because our children had been slaughtered in World War II by the regime using that coat of arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you about another symbol. You talk about the U symbol, which is maybe the symbol most closely associated with the Ustashas. Sir, while that symbol may have been used by individuals, extremists during 1990 and even after that, the U symbol was never used in any official capacity, neither by the HDZ nor by the Croatian government. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you -- excuse me, sir. I just want -- can you name me any specific examples of where the HDZ or the Croatian authorities officially used the U symbol?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying they used it officially --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, that would --

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: -- but you could see it everywhere on the walls in Croatia and the authorities never reacted to that. Tacitly, implicitly, they supported such symbols --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, let me stop you --

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: -- and these were largely re-introduced by the Croatian diaspora.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please focus carefully on my questions because in my question I said: While they may have been used by individuals, they weren't used in an official capacity. That's really the narrow issue I was focussed on and you've now answered that, so let me go on to the next -- the next point. In paragraph 5 you describe HDZ pre-election conventions where you say there were these Ustasha symbols. Would you agree with me, sir, that there were also extremists who used extremist imagery on the Serb side in political rallies during the first half of 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: I cannot deny that. There were individuals on the Serbian side as well, but such symbols on our side were not supported publicly and openly, especially not by the JNA or by our --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, you've answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: -- Krajina authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Also in paragraph 5 you refer to a specific incident where you say that a Serb was falsely accused of trying to assassinate Franjo Tudjman during a pre-election rally in Benkovac in March 1990. Just so we're clear, in fact what happened on that occasion was that Tudjman was speaking at a podium at a rally, and a Serb tried to attack him with a pistol. And then later on it was determined that that was a plastic pistol and it couldn't actually have killed him. That's the incident that you're referring to; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: It was a well-known event, very exploited by the Croatian media --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: -- irrespective of the fact that this was a plastic gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So am I correct that it was a plastic gun; that's what you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Later on they established that it was plastic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
