utterances.text: And then later there were rumours that this had been orchestrated, done on purpose, this was pre-electoral campaign used to -- contributed to Tudjman's cause --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you about specific questions; I'm not inviting you to go in and talk about other topics. Okay? We have a lot of ground to cover in a limited amount of time. So please -- you're obviously able to answer my questions and you're doing so, but then you go into other matters. So please focus with on me. Let me move your attention to paragraph 15 of your statement. There you describe a meeting on the 5th of July, 1990, in Knin and you suggest that Croatian MUP authorities went to Knin to force the police into adopting or agreeing to accept the chequer-board symbol, but that's a misleading, isn't it, sir. In fact, the Croatian authorities went there to discuss the issue. They didn't go there to use force. They went there to talk about this issue, right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: I don't know what information you have on that. In any case, when the police, armed to their teeth, comes to a Serbian area, well, everyone assumed that the -- what will ensue was to be an act of violence and that will resort to the use of force, and that's how it was interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Are you saying, sir, that on the 5th of July the Croatian police arrived armed to the teeth, or wasn't it in fact the case that -- I believe it was the deputy minister of the interior and other officials of the Croatian MUP came, political people, not -- not armed police but representatives came to discuss things in Knin on the 5th of July, 1990, right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't in Knin on those days. What I learned was that they came and that people assembled around the police station and nothing could be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So you weren't there and you don't know first-hand what happened on this occasion. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: No, I have no first-hand information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. After this 5 July 1990 meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you then accept, sir, that it was the politicians and not the army or police who came to Knin to discuss the issue, rather than to force it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I recall, the information was that the police were arriving as well as some others with them. But the people were anxious. What I need to say is that nothing of it can be made sense unless you draw parallels between the criminal independent state of Croatia in World War II and the newly formed Croatia that was being formed at the time using the same symbols. The people were afraid that World War II would repeat itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I -- I think you're going far beyond my question. I understand that you say that's what you were told, that's the information you got at the time. But following on questions by the Prosecution, you have said you were not there, you don't have any first-hand information about the point. Now, I'm trying to find out that if you now say you were not there, you don't have first-hand information, would you be prepared to accept the proposition by the Prosecution that in fact, contrary to what you heard, it was the politicians who came there to discuss the issue; it was not the police or the army coming to use force. And you can either say: Yes, I accept the proposition; or no, I don't accept the proposition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept for such a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this didn't change things in its essence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have answered my question, sir. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have just a couple more questions on this exact same topic. Maybe I should press ahead and take advantage of the last 20 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Dakic, after this meeting on the 5th of July, 1990, the Croatian authorities continued to work with the Serb policemen in Knin and elsewhere in Krajina, didn't they? In fact, I'll give you two specific examples and tell me if you can confirm them or deny them or if you just don't know. Shortly after that meeting the Croatian authorities appointed a Serb named Slobodan Vujko to be the chief of the Knin public security station, and another Serb, Dusan Latas, was made chief of the new Plaski police station; again, appointed by the Croatian authorities. Now, do you know anything about those two incidents? Can you confirm or deny them?

utterances.speaker: MILE DAKIC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that since I don't know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think now it's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Dakic, we've come to the end of the day for today. The matter is now going to be postponed to Wednesday, the 25th, at 9.00, in this same Courtroom II. Thank you very much. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
